questions.question: How would you structure a small vanilla-JavaScript app so that adding a feature does not break the UI?
questions.answer:
Keep one source of truth in plain data — an array of todos, an object of board columns, or a small store — and make the DOM a projection of that data. A render function reads the state and rebuilds the affected part of the UI; event handlers change state and then call render. Do not read values back out of the DOM to decide what the state is, because the DOM can be edited by the user, by CSS or by another script.

The loop is: event → update state → save (if needed) → render. Keep rendering deterministic and side-effect free, keep persistence separate, and keep network calls at the edges. This is the same idea frameworks formalise, but you can demonstrate it with createElement and textContent. It makes features additive: a new field is added to the state and to render, not patched into five click handlers.
key_points: One source of truth in data, not the DOM
Event → update state → render
Render is deterministic and derived from state
Keep persistence and network at the edges
New features become additive changes

questions.question: What async states should a weather dashboard model, and how do you prevent an older request from overwriting a newer one?
questions.answer:
Model at least four states: idle, loading, success (data) and error (message). Render each explicitly so the user never sees a blank panel with no explanation, and disable or ignore repeat submissions while loading. On success, store the data plus the city it belongs to, so a late response cannot be shown under the wrong heading.

To prevent stale overwrites, abort the previous request with an AbortController before starting a new one and ignore AbortError in the catch. Alternatively, tag each request with an incrementing id and only apply the response whose id matches the latest. Checking response.ok is mandatory because fetch resolves on 404/500. Finally, always clear the loading flag in a finally block (or after both branches) so a failure does not leave the UI stuck.
key_points: States: idle, loading, success, error
Abort the previous request with AbortController
Ignore AbortError; apply only the latest response
Check response.ok — fetch resolves on HTTP errors
Clear loading in finally

questions.question: You built a Todo app. What would you test first, and which parts would you mock?
questions.answer:
Test the pure logic first: adding an item does not mutate the input array, toggling flips only the matching id, and remaining counts incomplete items, including the empty list. These tests are fast and precise, and they cover the rules the UI depends on. Next, test the DOM wiring: submit the form, assert that the new item is rendered and persisted; click an item, assert the done state. Use jsdom and real DOM APIs.

Mock only boundaries you do not control: the network (fetch), the clock (timers) and storage if you want isolation. Do not mock the reducer you are testing. For the weather project, mock fetch to return ok:false and a rejection, and assert the error state. Coverage is a gap finder, not a goal: check the empty, error and duplicate paths rather than chasing 100%.
key_points: Test pure logic and edge cases first
Then DOM wiring with jsdom
Mock fetch, timers and storage only
Never mock the function under test
Use coverage to find gaps, not as a score

questions.question: Write matchRoute(routes, path) for the mini router. Each route has a name and a pattern with :params; return { name, params } or null.
key_points: Split path and pattern into segments
Compare segment counts first
Collect :params and decodeURIComponent
Return null for no match → caller renders 404
Render params with textContent
Concatenating message data into innerHTML is DOM XSS
onerror/onload handlers execute even though <script> may not
Use createElement + textContent + append

questions.answer:
It prints 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 binary64, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum carries a tiny error. Formatting that with toFixed(2) hides it, but comparisons and repeated additions accumulate more error. For money this is unacceptable.

Store integer minor units — paise or cents — and format only for display:

const expenses = [10, 20]; // paise
const total = expenses.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 30
new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(total / 100); // ₹0.30

Keep amounts as integers through storage and arithmetic, convert to major units only at the render boundary, and never parse formatted currency strings back into floats.
key_points: toFixed hides the error but does not fix arithmetic
Store integer paise/cents
Format with Intl only at the display boundary
Do not parse formatted currency back to float

questions.question: The infinite gallery fires three requests for page 1. The observer code checks isIntersecting. Why, and what guards are missing?
questions.answer:
IntersectionObserver can call the callback more than once while the sentinel remains visible, and it also fires immediately on observe(). If the callback starts a fetch without a synchronous guard, every call sees isIntersecting true and page still 1, so three requests go out before any of them resolves. The same happens on fast scrolling and on re-render if the observer is recreated.

Add a loading flag set synchronously before the await and cleared in finally, increment the page only after a successful append, and dedupe by id in case the server returns overlapping pages. Disconnect the observer when there is no next page, and handle errors so a failed request does not leave loading true forever. If the observer is recreated on every render, disconnect the old one first — otherwise handlers multiply and leak.
key_points: Observer fires on observe() and can repeat while visible
Set a synchronous loading guard before await
Increment page only after success
Dedupe ids for overlapping pages
Disconnect old observers and handle errors
